## Introduction

This document aims to provide an update on indications for mechanical thrombectomy in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) from emergent large vessel occlusion (ELVO) in the anterior circulation. This reflects new evidence building on the Society of NeuroInterventional Surgery (SNIS) recommendations published in 2015.[1](#ref-1) Recommendations herein supersede those of previous SNIS guidelines where overlap exists. Previous publications included an overview of prehospital care, a summary of the role of intravenous (IV) and intra-arterial (IA) therapies, a review of technical aspects of thrombectomy, and initial hospital management.[1–3](#ref-1) This guideline focuses on updated indications for thrombectomy of anterior circulation AIS. Evaluation and management of posterior circulation ELVO will be summarized in separate recommendations.

## Materials and methods

The Standards and Guidelines Committee of the SNIS, a multidisciplinary society representing the leaders in the field of endovascular therapy for neurovascular disease, prepared this document based on a comprehensive review of the available English language literature relating to the topic. Recommendations follow the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) classification of recommendation/level of evidence and definition of classes and levels of evidence used in American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) recommendations.[4](#ref-4) Throughout this document, we will refer to the specific selection criteria from the recent randomized trials and registries of modern thrombectomy approaches, which are summarized in [table 1](#T1).

Randomized trials and registries of modern approaches to thrombectomy

## Indications for thrombectomy

Defining the criteria to evaluate and select patients with ELVO for endovascular treatment is critically important, since between 3% and 22% of patients with AIS are potentially eligible for mechanical thrombectomy, depending on the specific selection criteria used.[5–7](#ref-5) Time of symptom onset (or last known well, magnitude of early ischemic change on initial imaging, clinical severity of stroke symptoms, pre-stroke level of functioning and anatomic location of the ELVO are the most important determinants of candidacy for mechanical thrombectomy.

### Time from symptom onset

MR CLEAN,[8](#ref-8) EXTEND-IA,[9](#ref-9) and SWIFT PRIME[10](#ref-10) proved the value of thrombectomy in anterior circulation AIS within the first 6 hours of symptom onset. Specifically, 33% of patients achieved a good clinical outcome (defined as modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score 0–2) with thrombectomy versus 19% with medical therapy in MR CLEAN (with an OR of 1.67). In EXTEND-IA, the respective outcomes were 71% versus 40% (generalized OR=2.0). In SWIFT PRIME, they were 60% versus 35% (calculated risk ratio 1.70). THRACE[11](#ref-11) provided additional data for thrombectomy up to 5 hours (53% of patients with thrombectomy achieved a good clinical outcome vs 42% with medical management, OR=1.55). The REVASCAT[12](#ref-12) and ESCAPE[13](#ref-13) trials provided initial evidence for the benefit of thrombectomy for patients with anterior circulation AIS up to 8 hours (44% with thrombectomy vs 28% with medical management, adjusted OR=2.1) and 12 hours (53% rate of good clinical outcome with thrombectomy versus 29% with medical management, rate ratio 1.8), respectively. A subgroup analysis of 59 patients enrolled within an extended time window (groin puncture within 6–12 hours) in ESCAPE showed similar treatment effects regardless of early and late windows.[14](#ref-14) A treatment effect favoring thrombectomy was seen across all clinical outcomes.

Two recent multicenter randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of mechanical thrombectomy initiated at a later time windows of up to 16 hours (endovascular therapy following imaging evaluation for ischemic stroke 3 [DEFUSE 3][15](#ref-15)) and 24 hours from symptom onset (diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI] or CT perfusion [CTP] assessment with clinical mismatch in the triage of wake-up and late presenting strokes undergoing neurointervention with Trevo [DAWN][16](#ref-16)) have shown that endovascular therapy is safe and highly effective in carefully selected patients with advanced CTP/magnetic resonance (MR) DWI-PWI imaging in comparison with medical management alone. In DEFUSE 3, 45% of patients achieved good clinical outcome with thrombectomy versus 17% with medical therapy, OR=2.67.[15](#ref-15) In DAWN, there was a similar treatment effect with rates of good clinical outcomes of 49% versus 13%, with an adjusted difference of 33%.[16](#ref-16)

At first glance, the results of DEFUSE 3 and DAWN suggest a ‘late time window paradox’ where patients treated with thrombectomy at a later time showed the largest absolute difference in good clinical outcome in comparison with earlier randomized thrombectomy trials. This finding seems to contradict the time-dependency effect of thrombectomy in which each 1 hour delay to reperfusion lowers the chances of good clinical outcome observed in HERMES.[17](#ref-17) However, a more critical concept illustrated by DEFUSE 3 and DAWN was that collateral flow, in addition to elapsed time, together contribute to duration of tissue viability during ischemia. The use of strict imaging-based selection criteria in DEFUSE 3 and DAWN allowed for the surrogate assessment of collaterals, which now represents an important variable in selection of patients for thrombectomy.

While RCTs are considered ‘the gold standard’ for establishing clinical evidence, their design and applicability to daily clinical practice can be significantly limited by the trials’ selection criteria. Registries provide additional useful information by including a wider range of patients that can potentially serve to validate the findings of RCTs. The TRACK[18](#ref-18) and NASA[19](#ref-19) registries assessed real-world experience with thrombectomy without any specific restriction in time from symptom onset to treatment. Both registries showed rates of clinical outcomes comparable to the major RCTs (48% and 42% rates of good clinical outcome in TRACK and NASA, respectively). Combined, 33% of patients from both registries were treated with thrombectomy beyond the first 6 hours, and the safety and efficacy of this treatment was equal to that of treatment performed within 0–6 hours.[20](#ref-20) No specific imaging criteria or modalities were required in TRACK and NASA; imaging-based patient selection was left to the discretion of each participating site.

Therefore, there are high-level data from multiple RCTs and registries in support of thrombectomy in appropriately selected patients, up to 24 hours from symptom onset or last known well, including wake-up strokes. There is insufficient evidence to evaluate the safety and efficacy of thrombectomy >24 hours from symptom onset. Presently, only limited experience with thrombectomy of anterior circulation ELVO after 24 hours has been reported.[21](#ref-21)

### Imaging criteria for thrombectomy

RCTs have used a number of radiographic selection criteria to determine candidacy for thrombectomy. Specific imaging criteria from these RCTs are summarized in [table 1](#T1). The primary purpose of imaging in patient selection is to exclude patients unlikely to benefit or for whom thrombectomy may be harmful. Selection criteria for the late-window trials (>6 hours) were more selective than the <6 hours RCTs. For thrombectomy <6 hours, there are insufficient data to establish the superiority of one particular imaging modality. These include non-contrast CT, MR DWI, multiphase CT angiography (mCTA) collateral imaging, and advanced CT/MR perfusion imaging with standardized postprocessing techniques. Various imaging criteria such as the Alberta Stroke Programme Early CT Score (ASPECTS) 6–10, MRI DWI ASPECTS 5–10, moderate-to-good collateral status on mCTA (>50% middle cerebral artery [MCA] territory), small (<50–70 mL) core infarct volumes, and significant penumbra to core mismatch on perfusion imaging have been used as selection criteria in study subjects with anterior circulation stroke and symptom onset up to 6 hours who qualify for thrombectomy.

In patients 6–24 hours, MR DWI-PWI and CTP imaging are highly accurate in selecting patients for thrombectomy when based on criteria used in DEFUSE 3 and DAWN. However, as discussed earlier, both trials, because of restrictive radiographic selection criteria, limit their generalizability to many patients with ELVO. For example, a single-center study of patients presenting 6–24 hours after last known well showed that 70% of these patients with anterior circulation ELVO were DAWN and/or DEFUSE 3 ineligible.[22](#ref-22) Yet, thrombectomy in these patients resulted in rates of good clinical outcomes comparable to those of DAWN and DEFUSE 3 eligible patients.[22](#ref-22)

Data from the early HERMES collaboration of five RCTs,[23](#ref-23) subgroup analyses of THRACE,[24](#ref-24) and matched case–control studies indicated that thrombectomy may be beneficial even in patients with ischemic strokes presenting with large core infarct volumes, such as those with CT/MRI ASPECTS 3–5 or MRI DWI and CTP estimated core volumes of >50–70 mL.[25–27](#ref-25) The latest HERMES collaboration analysis based on individual patient data from RCTs (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA, SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT, THRACE, and PISTE) showed that thrombectomy led to better clinical outcomes at 90 days across a broad range of imaging categories, including ASPECTS <6 (OR=1.58 for ASPECTS 5–7 and OR=2.15 for ASPECTS 0–4) and infarcts affecting >1/3 of MCA territory (OR 1.7), supporting the value of thrombectomy in some patients with large infarcts at baseline.[28](#ref-28) However, thrombectomy in patients with such unfavorable imaging profiles had higher rates of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage than in the control group. A separate HERMES collaboration analysis of seven RCTs also confirmed that thrombectomy administered within 0–6 hours of symptom onset remained beneficial in patients with a large (>70 mL) ischemic core measured with CTP or MRI.[29](#ref-29)

### Location of large vessel occlusion

The anatomic definition of an ELVO is variable.[30](#ref-30) For the purpose of this document, any arterial location or lesion that can be safely selectively catheterized with modern endovascular devices will be referred to as an ELVO. Rigorous clinical trial data support mechanical thrombectomy in patients with intracranial and extracranial occlusions of the internal carotid artery (ICA), including tandem or isolated occlusion of the M1 and M2 segments of the MCA ([table 1](#T1)). Patients with M2 occlusions were also included for thrombectomy in the MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT, and THERAPY trials, although in limited numbers.

The benefit of thrombectomy for more distal MCA occlusions, such as the M3 segments, or anterior cerebral artery occlusions is unclear despite a number of studies evaluating the outcomes of thrombectomy in these patients. This is due to a paucity of data representative of this cohort. Although studies indicate that thrombectomy may be safe and effective in patients with distal anterior circulation ELVO, evidence also suggests an increased risk profile with mechanical interventions, such as vessel perforation and vasospasm.[31–34](#ref-31) Furthermore, although the natural history of distal occlusions is probably, on average, more favorable than proximal occlusions, the level of disability may still be significant and warrants clarification.

### Stroke severity

When determining eligibility for thrombectomy, stroke severity should be assessed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS).[35](#ref-35) Use of a standardized scale directly quantifies the degree of neurological deficit, facilitates communication, helps to identify patients for thrombolytic or mechanical intervention, allows objective measurement of changing clinical status, and may identify those at higher risk for complications such as intracerebral hemorrhage. There was significant variability in the NIHSS score thresholds used for inclusion in recent RCTs for thrombectomy. The MR CLEAN trial had the lowest NIHSS score threshold of 2, ESCAPE and EXTEND-IA set no specific NIHSS score thresholds, but required the symptoms to be ‘disabling’, whereas other trials had variable ranges from an NIHSS score of 6 to 10 ([table 1](#T1)). Because several trials independently validated an NIHSS threshold of 6 (SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT and DEFUSE 3), an NIHSS score of >6 may serve as a working criterion of clinical severity when considering thrombectomy in anterior circulation AIS. However, patients presenting with anterior circulation ELVO and NIHSS score <6, but with otherwise disabling symptoms such as isolated aphasia, should be considered for thrombectomy. Several studies describe a poor natural history in this cohort, with sometimes eventual worsening of neurologic deficits and functional independence in up to a quarter of patients.[36](#ref-36) More data on this topic are needed ([table 2](#T2)).[37–40](#ref-37)

Natural history (medical therapy only, no IV tPA) and thrombectomy outcomes in patients with ELVO and mild symptoms

### Thrombectomy and intravenous thrombolysis

In recent RCTs of thrombectomy, patients eligible for IV thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA; alteplase) before thrombectomy received both treatments ([table 1](#T1)). Although there is accumulating evidence suggesting that administering IV rtPA in thrombectomy-eligible patients may be futile,[41–43](#ref-41) there are also data suggesting that it may be beneficial in patients with ELVO.[44](#ref-44) This topic is complicated by evidence showing that the efficacy of IV tPA depends on thrombus location; proximal thrombi are less likely to respond to thrombolysis, whereas tPA has a higher likelihood of inducing recanalization at more distally located thrombi.[45 46](#ref-45) Thus, future trials comparing thrombectomy with thrombolysis may need to include analysis by thrombus location. A RCT comparing the safety and efficacy of thrombectomy with rtPA versus thrombectomy alone is currently underway in Europe (SWIFT DIRECT, ClinicalTrials.gov [NCT03192332](/lookup/external-ref?link_type=CLINTRIALGOV&access_num=NCT03192332&atom=%2Fneurintsurg%2F11%2F3%2F215.atom)). Additional studies are being considered evaluating lytics other than alteplase in select patients with ELVO with an extended time window. Presently, in patients with anterior circulation ELVO who are eligible for both treatment approaches, IV rtPA should be given. However, treatment with IV rtPA should not delay the initiation of thrombectomy in these patients.

### Age and baseline level of functioning

Significant pre-existing disability often precludes favorable clinical outcomes despite successful thrombectomy. Whether it is due to frailty, poor nutritional status, limited baseline functional capacity, or comorbidities, such patients would, in theory, have almost nothing to gain from thrombectomy. No randomized data exist for thrombectomy in patients with mRS score >1, but this may be a topic of interest for future investigators. On the other hand, multiple studies evaluating thrombectomy in elderly patients have showed mixed but promising results.[47–49](#ref-47) The HERMES collaboration analysis of patient-level data of five RCTs showed significant benefit of thrombectomy in patients aged >80 years with a common OR of 3.68.[23](#ref-23)

## Recommendations

### Time from symptom onset

For anterior circulation AIS, thrombectomy is indicated in select patients up to 16 hours from symptom onset or time last known well for unwitnessed strokes, including wake-up strokes [class I, level A], and is indicated in select patients up to 24 hours from last known normal [class IIa, level B]. This replaces the 2015 SNIS guidelines in which thrombectomy recommendations were limited to the first 6 hours of symptom onset.

### Imaging

In patients with anterior circulation AIS within the first 6 hours of symptom onset and *either* CT ASPECTS ≥6, MRI DWI ASPECTS ≥6, moderate-to-good collateral status on mCTA (>50% MCA territory), small (<50–70 mL) core infarct volumes, and/or significant penumbral to core mismatch on advanced perfusion imaging (CTP or MRI-DWI-PWI), thrombectomy is indicated [class I, level A].

Thrombectomy may be reasonable within the first 6 hours of symptom onset in patients with a large core infarct volume such as CT ASPECTS of <6, MRI DWI or CTP-estimated core volume >70 mL [class IIa, level A].

In patients with anterior circulation AIS due to intracranial ICA and/or M1 occlusion within 6–24 hours of symptom onset who meet the advanced MRI DWI-PWI or CTP imaging criteria for DAWN or DEFUSE 3, thrombectomy is indicated [class I, level B].

Thrombectomy may be indicated in carefully selected patients with anterior circulation AIS within 6–24 hours of symptom onset who do not meet imaging criteria for DAWN and DEFUSE 3 but otherwise have a ‘favorable’ imaging profile such as CT ASPECTS of 6–10, MRI DWI ASPECTS of 6–10, moderate-to-good collateral status on mCTA, or small (<70 mL) core infarct on advanced MRI DWI-PWI or CTP imaging [class IIb, level B-NR (non-randomized)].

### Location of ELVO

Thrombectomy is indicated in patients with occlusions of the ICA (including intracranial, cervical segments or tandem occlusion) and M1/M2 MCA [class I, level A]. This replaces the 2015 SNIS guidelines in which thrombectomy recommendations were limited to ICA and MCA M1 LVO locations.

The benefit of thrombectomy in more distal segments, such as MCA M3 or anterior cerebral artery is unclear. Thrombectomy of such patients may be reasonable in some cases and should be considered on a case-by-case basis [class IIb, level B-NR].

### Stroke severity

Thrombectomy is indicated in patients with anterior circulation ELVO with NIHSS score ≥6 [class I, level A].

Thrombectomy may be considered in patients with anterior circulation AIS and NIHSS score <6 when associated with disabling symptoms [class IIa, level B-NR]. However, care should be taken when treating these patients to keep complication and hemorrhagic rates below those reported in RCTs.

### Age and baseline level of functioning

Age >80 years should not be used as a contraindication for thrombectomy [class IIa, level A].

The benefit of thrombectomy in patients with baseline mRS score >1 is unknown.

Randomized trials and registries of modern approaches to thrombectomy

## Indications for thrombectomy

Defining the criteria to evaluate and select patients with ELVO for endovascular treatment is critically important, since between 3% and 22% of patients with AIS are potentially eligible for mechanical thrombectomy, depending on the specific selection criteria used.[5–7](#ref-5) Time of symptom onset (or last known well, magnitude of early ischemic change on initial imaging, clinical severity of stroke symptoms, pre-stroke level of functioning and anatomic location of the ELVO are the most important determinants of candidacy for mechanical thrombectomy.

### Time from symptom onset

MR CLEAN,[8](#ref-8) EXTEND-IA,[9](#ref-9) and SWIFT PRIME[10](#ref-10) proved the value of thrombectomy in anterior circulation AIS within the first 6 hours of symptom onset. Specifically, 33% of patients achieved a good clinical outcome (defined as modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score 0–2) with thrombectomy versus 19% with medical therapy in MR CLEAN (with an OR of 1.67). In EXTEND-IA, the respective outcomes were 71% versus 40% (generalized OR=2.0). In SWIFT PRIME, they were 60% versus 35% (calculated risk ratio 1.70). THRACE[11](#ref-11) provided additional data for thrombectomy up to 5 hours (53% of patients with thrombectomy achieved a good clinical outcome vs 42% with medical management, OR=1.55). The REVASCAT[12](#ref-12) and ESCAPE[13](#ref-13) trials provided initial evidence for the benefit of thrombectomy for patients with anterior circulation AIS up to 8 hours (44% with thrombectomy vs 28% with medical management, adjusted OR=2.1) and 12 hours (53% rate of good clinical outcome with thrombectomy versus 29% with medical management, rate ratio 1.8), respectively. A subgroup analysis of 59 patients enrolled within an extended time window (groin puncture within 6–12 hours) in ESCAPE showed similar treatment effects regardless of early and late windows.[14](#ref-14) A treatment effect favoring thrombectomy was seen across all clinical outcomes.

Two recent multicenter randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of mechanical thrombectomy initiated at a later time windows of up to 16 hours (endovascular therapy following imaging evaluation for ischemic stroke 3 [DEFUSE 3][15](#ref-15)) and 24 hours from symptom onset (diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI] or CT perfusion [CTP] assessment with clinical mismatch in the triage of wake-up and late presenting strokes undergoing neurointervention with Trevo [DAWN][16](#ref-16)) have shown that endovascular therapy is safe and highly effective in carefully selected patients with advanced CTP/magnetic resonance (MR) DWI-PWI imaging in comparison with medical management alone. In DEFUSE 3, 45% of patients achieved good clinical outcome with thrombectomy versus 17% with medical therapy, OR=2.67.[15](#ref-15) In DAWN, there was a similar treatment effect with rates of good clinical outcomes of 49% versus 13%, with an adjusted difference of 33%.[16](#ref-16)

At first glance, the results of DEFUSE 3 and DAWN suggest a ‘late time window paradox’ where patients treated with thrombectomy at a later time showed the largest absolute difference in good clinical outcome in comparison with earlier randomized thrombectomy trials. This finding seems to contradict the time-dependency effect of thrombectomy in which each 1 hour delay to reperfusion lowers the chances of good clinical outcome observed in HERMES.[17](#ref-17) However, a more critical concept illustrated by DEFUSE 3 and DAWN was that collateral flow, in addition to elapsed time, together contribute to duration of tissue viability during ischemia. The use of strict imaging-based selection criteria in DEFUSE 3 and DAWN allowed for the surrogate assessment of collaterals, which now represents an important variable in selection of patients for thrombectomy.

While RCTs are considered ‘the gold standard’ for establishing clinical evidence, their design and applicability to daily clinical practice can be significantly limited by the trials’ selection criteria. Registries provide additional useful information by including a wider range of patients that can potentially serve to validate the findings of RCTs. The TRACK[18](#ref-18) and NASA[19](#ref-19) registries assessed real-world experience with thrombectomy without any specific restriction in time from symptom onset to treatment. Both registries showed rates of clinical outcomes comparable to the major RCTs (48% and 42% rates of good clinical outcome in TRACK and NASA, respectively). Combined, 33% of patients from both registries were treated with thrombectomy beyond the first 6 hours, and the safety and efficacy of this treatment was equal to that of treatment performed within 0–6 hours.[20](#ref-20) No specific imaging criteria or modalities were required in TRACK and NASA; imaging-based patient selection was left to the discretion of each participating site.

Therefore, there are high-level data from multiple RCTs and registries in support of thrombectomy in appropriately selected patients, up to 24 hours from symptom onset or last known well, including wake-up strokes. There is insufficient evidence to evaluate the safety and efficacy of thrombectomy >24 hours from symptom onset. Presently, only limited experience with thrombectomy of anterior circulation ELVO after 24 hours has been reported.[21](#ref-21)

### Imaging criteria for thrombectomy

RCTs have used a number of radiographic selection criteria to determine candidacy for thrombectomy. Specific imaging criteria from these RCTs are summarized in [table 1](#T1). The primary purpose of imaging in patient selection is to exclude patients unlikely to benefit or for whom thrombectomy may be harmful. Selection criteria for the late-window trials (>6 hours) were more selective than the <6 hours RCTs. For thrombectomy <6 hours, there are insufficient data to establish the superiority of one particular imaging modality. These include non-contrast CT, MR DWI, multiphase CT angiography (mCTA) collateral imaging, and advanced CT/MR perfusion imaging with standardized postprocessing techniques. Various imaging criteria such as the Alberta Stroke Programme Early CT Score (ASPECTS) 6–10, MRI DWI ASPECTS 5–10, moderate-to-good collateral status on mCTA (>50% middle cerebral artery [MCA] territory), small (<50–70 mL) core infarct volumes, and significant penumbra to core mismatch on perfusion imaging have been used as selection criteria in study subjects with anterior circulation stroke and symptom onset up to 6 hours who qualify for thrombectomy.

In patients 6–24 hours, MR DWI-PWI and CTP imaging are highly accurate in selecting patients for thrombectomy when based on criteria used in DEFUSE 3 and DAWN. However, as discussed earlier, both trials, because of restrictive radiographic selection criteria, limit their generalizability to many patients with ELVO. For example, a single-center study of patients presenting 6–24 hours after last known well showed that 70% of these patients with anterior circulation ELVO were DAWN and/or DEFUSE 3 ineligible.[22](#ref-22) Yet, thrombectomy in these patients resulted in rates of good clinical outcomes comparable to those of DAWN and DEFUSE 3 eligible patients.[22](#ref-22)

Data from the early HERMES collaboration of five RCTs,[23](#ref-23) subgroup analyses of THRACE,[24](#ref-24) and matched case–control studies indicated that thrombectomy may be beneficial even in patients with ischemic strokes presenting with large core infarct volumes, such as those with CT/MRI ASPECTS 3–5 or MRI DWI and CTP estimated core volumes of >50–70 mL.[25–27](#ref-25) The latest HERMES collaboration analysis based on individual patient data from RCTs (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA, SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT, THRACE, and PISTE) showed that thrombectomy led to better clinical outcomes at 90 days across a broad range of imaging categories, including ASPECTS <6 (OR=1.58 for ASPECTS 5–7 and OR=2.15 for ASPECTS 0–4) and infarcts affecting >1/3 of MCA territory (OR 1.7), supporting the value of thrombectomy in some patients with large infarcts at baseline.[28](#ref-28) However, thrombectomy in patients with such unfavorable imaging profiles had higher rates of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage than in the control group. A separate HERMES collaboration analysis of seven RCTs also confirmed that thrombectomy administered within 0–6 hours of symptom onset remained beneficial in patients with a large (>70 mL) ischemic core measured with CTP or MRI.[29](#ref-29)

### Location of large vessel occlusion

The anatomic definition of an ELVO is variable.[30](#ref-30) For the purpose of this document, any arterial location or lesion that can be safely selectively catheterized with modern endovascular devices will be referred to as an ELVO. Rigorous clinical trial data support mechanical thrombectomy in patients with intracranial and extracranial occlusions of the internal carotid artery (ICA), including tandem or isolated occlusion of the M1 and M2 segments of the MCA ([table 1](#T1)). Patients with M2 occlusions were also included for thrombectomy in the MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT, and THERAPY trials, although in limited numbers.

The benefit of thrombectomy for more distal MCA occlusions, such as the M3 segments, or anterior cerebral artery occlusions is unclear despite a number of studies evaluating the outcomes of thrombectomy in these patients. This is due to a paucity of data representative of this cohort. Although studies indicate that thrombectomy may be safe and effective in patients with distal anterior circulation ELVO, evidence also suggests an increased risk profile with mechanical interventions, such as vessel perforation and vasospasm.[31–34](#ref-31) Furthermore, although the natural history of distal occlusions is probably, on average, more favorable than proximal occlusions, the level of disability may still be significant and warrants clarification.

### Stroke severity

When determining eligibility for thrombectomy, stroke severity should be assessed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS).[35](#ref-35) Use of a standardized scale directly quantifies the degree of neurological deficit, facilitates communication, helps to identify patients for thrombolytic or mechanical intervention, allows objective measurement of changing clinical status, and may identify those at higher risk for complications such as intracerebral hemorrhage. There was significant variability in the NIHSS score thresholds used for inclusion in recent RCTs for thrombectomy. The MR CLEAN trial had the lowest NIHSS score threshold of 2, ESCAPE and EXTEND-IA set no specific NIHSS score thresholds, but required the symptoms to be ‘disabling’, whereas other trials had variable ranges from an NIHSS score of 6 to 10 ([table 1](#T1)). Because several trials independently validated an NIHSS threshold of 6 (SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT and DEFUSE 3), an NIHSS score of >6 may serve as a working criterion of clinical severity when considering thrombectomy in anterior circulation AIS. However, patients presenting with anterior circulation ELVO and NIHSS score <6, but with otherwise disabling symptoms such as isolated aphasia, should be considered for thrombectomy. Several studies describe a poor natural history in this cohort, with sometimes eventual worsening of neurologic deficits and functional independence in up to a quarter of patients.[36](#ref-36) More data on this topic are needed ([table 2](#T2)).[37–40](#ref-37)

Natural history (medical therapy only, no IV tPA) and thrombectomy outcomes in patients with ELVO and mild symptoms

### Thrombectomy and intravenous thrombolysis

In recent RCTs of thrombectomy, patients eligible for IV thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA; alteplase) before thrombectomy received both treatments ([table 1](#T1)). Although there is accumulating evidence suggesting that administering IV rtPA in thrombectomy-eligible patients may be futile,[41–43](#ref-41) there are also data suggesting that it may be beneficial in patients with ELVO.[44](#ref-44) This topic is complicated by evidence showing that the efficacy of IV tPA depends on thrombus location; proximal thrombi are less likely to respond to thrombolysis, whereas tPA has a higher likelihood of inducing recanalization at more distally located thrombi.[45 46](#ref-45) Thus, future trials comparing thrombectomy with thrombolysis may need to include analysis by thrombus location. A RCT comparing the safety and efficacy of thrombectomy with rtPA versus thrombectomy alone is currently underway in Europe (SWIFT DIRECT, ClinicalTrials.gov [NCT03192332](/lookup/external-ref?link_type=CLINTRIALGOV&access_num=NCT03192332&atom=%2Fneurintsurg%2F11%2F3%2F215.atom)). Additional studies are being considered evaluating lytics other than alteplase in select patients with ELVO with an extended time window. Presently, in patients with anterior circulation ELVO who are eligible for both treatment approaches, IV rtPA should be given. However, treatment with IV rtPA should not delay the initiation of thrombectomy in these patients.

### Age and baseline level of functioning

Significant pre-existing disability often precludes favorable clinical outcomes despite successful thrombectomy. Whether it is due to frailty, poor nutritional status, limited baseline functional capacity, or comorbidities, such patients would, in theory, have almost nothing to gain from thrombectomy. No randomized data exist for thrombectomy in patients with mRS score >1, but this may be a topic of interest for future investigators. On the other hand, multiple studies evaluating thrombectomy in elderly patients have showed mixed but promising results.[47–49](#ref-47) The HERMES collaboration analysis of patient-level data of five RCTs showed significant benefit of thrombectomy in patients aged >80 years with a common OR of 3.68.[23](#ref-23)

## Recommendations

### Time from symptom onset

For anterior circulation AIS, thrombectomy is indicated in select patients up to 16 hours from symptom onset or time last known well for unwitnessed strokes, including wake-up strokes [class I, level A], and is indicated in select patients up to 24 hours from last known normal [class IIa, level B]. This replaces the 2015 SNIS guidelines in which thrombectomy recommendations were limited to the first 6 hours of symptom onset.

### Imaging

In patients with anterior circulation AIS within the first 6 hours of symptom onset and *either* CT ASPECTS ≥6, MRI DWI ASPECTS ≥6, moderate-to-good collateral status on mCTA (>50% MCA territory), small (<50–70 mL) core infarct volumes, and/or significant penumbral to core mismatch on advanced perfusion imaging (CTP or MRI-DWI-PWI), thrombectomy is indicated [class I, level A].

Thrombectomy may be reasonable within the first 6 hours of symptom onset in patients with a large core infarct volume such as CT ASPECTS of <6, MRI DWI or CTP-estimated core volume >70 mL [class IIa, level A].

In patients with anterior circulation AIS due to intracranial ICA and/or M1 occlusion within 6–24 hours of symptom onset who meet the advanced MRI DWI-PWI or CTP imaging criteria for DAWN or DEFUSE 3, thrombectomy is indicated [class I, level B].

Thrombectomy may be indicated in carefully selected patients with anterior circulation AIS within 6–24 hours of symptom onset who do not meet imaging criteria for DAWN and DEFUSE 3 but otherwise have a ‘favorable’ imaging profile such as CT ASPECTS of 6–10, MRI DWI ASPECTS of 6–10, moderate-to-good collateral status on mCTA, or small (<70 mL) core infarct on advanced MRI DWI-PWI or CTP imaging [class IIb, level B-NR (non-randomized)].

### Location of ELVO

Thrombectomy is indicated in patients with occlusions of the ICA (including intracranial, cervical segments or tandem occlusion) and M1/M2 MCA [class I, level A]. This replaces the 2015 SNIS guidelines in which thrombectomy recommendations were limited to ICA and MCA M1 LVO locations.

The benefit of thrombectomy in more distal segments, such as MCA M3 or anterior cerebral artery is unclear. Thrombectomy of such patients may be reasonable in some cases and should be considered on a case-by-case basis [class IIb, level B-NR].

### Stroke severity

Thrombectomy is indicated in patients with anterior circulation ELVO with NIHSS score ≥6 [class I, level A].

Thrombectomy may be considered in patients with anterior circulation AIS and NIHSS score <6 when associated with disabling symptoms [class IIa, level B-NR]. However, care should be taken when treating these patients to keep complication and hemorrhagic rates below those reported in RCTs.

### Age and baseline level of functioning

Age >80 years should not be used as a contraindication for thrombectomy [class IIa, level A].

The benefit of thrombectomy in patients with baseline mRS score >1 is unknown.

The prospect of receiving mechanical thrombectomy for acute stroke is associated with geographic proximity and how close people are to hospitals offering this treatment. Changing treatment window time will allow patients who were excluded for unknown reason or late arriving for medical care to still benefit from thrombectomy. Faster time to treatment remain critical for the achievement of the best possible outcomes. Thrombectomy is safe with careful selection of patients and in experienced operators with a dedicated interventional team. Therefore, thrombectomy delivery will need to continue to improve [...] This limited treatment window has led to interest in endovascular therapy to extend the treatment window for acute ischemic stroke. In 2015, five randomized clinical trials searched for efficacy of mechanical thrombectomy in patients with acute stroke caused large vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation (3). Their findings demonstrated that critical imaging analysis, workflow modification, and newer generation thrombectomy devices were beneficial in treatment of ischemic stroke using endovascular treatment over standard medical care. These trials changed guidelines that endovascular treatment is a highly effective therapy across all subgroups if performed within 6 hours of stroke presentation. * A new DAWN for extended window thrombectomy in ischemic stroke: an editorial on the DAWN trial

A new DAWN for extended window thrombectomy in ischemic stroke: an editorial on the DAWN trial

![](https://cdn.amegroups.cn/static/mirror/crossmark/widget/v2.0/CROSSMARK_Color_horizontal.svg)

Editorial

# A new DAWN for extended window thrombectomy in ischemic stroke: an editorial on the DAWN trial

Chen Lin, Muhammad Mansour Ali Adham Mansour

Department of Neurology, Northwestern University, IL, USA

*Correspondence to:* Chen Lin. Department of Neurology Northwestern University, 633 Clark St, Evanston, IL 60208, USA. Email: chen.lin1@Northwestern.edu.

*Comment on:* [Nogueira RG, Jadhav AP, Haussen DC, *et al*. Thrombectomy 6 to 24 Hours after Stroke with a Mismatch between De cit and Infarct. N Engl J Med 2018;378:11-21.](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29129157)

---

Received: 18 December 2017; Accepted: 21 December 2017; Published: 21 January 2018.

doi: 10.21037/jeccm.2017.12.10

---

Stroke is one of the leading causes of long-term disability in the United States and around the world ([1](#B1)). Most of all strokes are ischemic, in which the brain’s blood supply is obstructed. In the majority of stroke survivors greater than 65 years old, this can significantly impact their independence and mobility ([1](#B1)). Clinical trials in stroke have been designed to reduce mortality and morbidity in populations at high risk. Patients arriving at a hospital within 3–4.5 h of their symptom onset can qualify for acute thrombolysis which leads to improved function after a stroke ([2](#B2)). Considered the gold standard in acute stroke therapy, IV-alteplase is the only FDA-approved treatment for ischemic strokes, but needs to be used within a limited therapeutic time window.

This limited treatment window has led to interest in endovascular therapy to extend the treatment window for acute ischemic stroke. In 2015, five randomized clinical trials searched for efficacy of mechanical thrombectomy in patients with acute stroke caused large vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation ([3](#B3)). Their findings demonstrated that critical imaging analysis, workflow modification, and newer generation thrombectomy devices were beneficial in treatment of ischemic stroke using endovascular treatment over standard medical care. These trials changed guidelines that endovascular treatment is a highly effective therapy across all subgroups if performed within 6 hours of stroke presentation. Of the 5 trials, only 2 had therapy windows beyond 6 h. The REVASCAT trial recruited eligible patients within 8 h after the onset of symptoms ([4](#B4)). Results showed thrombectomy within 8 h of onset, reduced the severity of disability and higher rates of functional independence. However, over 87.4% of their treatment groups were performed within 6 h. The ESCAPE trial enrolled up to 12 h after symptom onset with a small infarct core. Their median time from stroke onset to treatment reperfusion was about 4 h ([5](#B5)). Despite these two trials, there was insufficient evidence that endovascular therapy window beyond 6 h had significant treatment effect to limit disability.

The DWI or CTP Assessment with Clinical Mismatch in the Triage of Wake-Up and Late Presenting Strokes Undergoing Neurointervention with Trevo (DAWN) trial was designed to answer two lingering questions: (I) the unclear benefit of endovascular treatment beyond 6 h and (II) how to carefully select for patients based on a clinical-radiologic mismatch to salvage with reperfusion therapy ([6](#B6)). The DAWN clinical trial is an international, randomized controlled research study investigating the benefits of thrombectomy 6–24 h after stroke onset. Instead of looking at penumbral volume or only stroke lesion burden, DAWN investigators selected patients based on a clinical-radiologic mismatch. Patients were selected based on three groups. The first was ≥80 years old, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) ≥10, and core volume infarct <21 cc. The second group was <80 years old, NIHSS ≥10, and core infarct volume <31 cc. Finally, the last group was <80 years old, NIHSS >20, and core infarct volume of 31–51 cc. Patients meeting these criteria could then be randomized 1:1 to either thrombectomy or medical control therapy. DAWN was conducted across 26 centers in Europe, Australia, the US, and Canada. The study enrolled a total of 206 patients from September 2014 through February 2017. To qualify as a participating center, ≥40 mechanical thrombectomy procedures had to be performed annually at the centers. Dedicated stroke or neurointensive care units would also be required to admit enrolled patients. Local institute guidelines directed medical care if patients did not qualify for thrombectomy. Patients were followed for 90 days and the primary efficacy endpoint was assessed via utility-weighted modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and dichotomized mRS. The dichotomized mRS was originally a secondary outcome, but the investigators were asked by the FDA to change to a primary outcome. Choosing utility-weighted mRS for disability after stroke over traditional mRS was meant to address some concerns over limitations of power with the traditional mRS. Utility-weighted mRS is theoretically thought to capture better treatment effects and maintain statistical power while improving scale interpretability then when analyzed ordinally ([7](#B7)). The median baseline NIHSS score in their cohort was 17 for both groups. The first primary endpoint for the utility-weighted mRS at 90 days for the thrombectomy group was 5.5 versus 3.4 in the control group, with higher numbers representing better outcomes. In the second primary endpoint, 48.6% of thrombectomy patients were independent at 3 months compared to 13.1% in the medical arm. The rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage nor 90-day mortality did not differ significantly between the study groups.

While the results are extremely favorable for treating ischemic stroke up to 24 h in a carefully selected group of patients, there are still concerns. A major question of the study is that investigators did not report screening numbers in how many patients would truly present with the trial’s selection criteria. If new thrombectomy centers are to be created based on DAWN results, there remain several questions as to if creating a better system of care would be more beneficial. Establishing new centers performing thrombectomy procedures require a lot of resources including: a specific perfusion software used in this study (RAPID) that can be cost-prohibitive; dedicated stroke units and neurointensive units are also critical in improved outcomes. The centers in this study also required a certain amount of expertise to obtain these improved outcomes. Mechanical thrombectomy is associated with intra-procedural or post-operative complications, which need to be minimized and effectively managed to maximize the benefits of thrombectomy. Procedural complications include: access-site problems (vessel/nerve injury, access-site hematoma, and groin infection); device-related complications; symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage; subarachnoid hemorrhage; embolization to new or target vessel territory. Some complications are life-threatening, and many lead to increased length of stay in intensive care and stroke units. Complications increase costs and delay the commencement of rehabilitation. Fortunately, in the results, it seems that complication rates are similar between the two treatment complications. However, these issues point to the importance in determining whether creating new systems of care and centers based on current DAWN data is a practical use of resources to better select for patients within the extended treatment period. More information is needed in how often patients meet DAWN inclusion criteria before generalizing results and forming new guidelines for treatment.

The results from DAWN are truly positive and potentially game-changing and safe for treatment of select ischemic stroke patients presenting up to 24 h. With future extended-window interventional trials on the horizon, including DEFUSE-3, changes in stroke treatment guidelines will likely be forthcoming again. If we can determine how many stroke patients can benefit from these results, we can start developing better care that includes improved access to imaging (CT head, CT angiogram, and CT perfusion imaging) and selecting patients appropriate for endovascular treatment. CT angiography is not routinely available in all hospitals. Perfusion imaging for acute stroke is also not routinely done, even in stroke centers, and typically requires selection for high-risk large vessel occlusion patients. Further studies need to be done on how many centers offer 24 h endovascular clot retrieval and its geographic distribution. The prospect of receiving mechanical thrombectomy for acute stroke is associated with geographic proximity and how close people are to hospitals offering this treatment. Changing treatment window time will allow patients who were excluded for unknown reason or late arriving for medical care to still benefit from thrombectomy. Faster time to treatment remain critical for the achievement of the best possible outcomes. Thrombectomy is safe with careful selection of patients and in experienced operators with a dedicated interventional team. Therefore, thrombectomy delivery will need to continue to improve in both specific centers and their systems of care with teams.

## Abstract

Please see the [Editorial Comment](https://www.ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28814) by Shalini A. Amukotuwa, discussing this article.

Endovascular thrombectomy has become the standard-of-care treatment for carefully selected patients with acute ischemic stroke due to a large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation. Neuroimaging plays a vital role in determining patient eligibility for thrombectomy, both in the early (0–6 hours from symptom onset) and late (> 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset) time windows. Various neuroimaging algorithms are used to determine thrombectomy eligibility, and each algorithm must be optimized for institutional workflow. In this review, we describe common imaging modalities and recommended algorithms for the evaluation of patients for endovascular thrombectomy. We also discuss emerging patient populations who might qualify for thrombectomy in the coming years.

## HIGHLIGHTS

▪ _Neuroimaging for patient selection for thrombectomy should include exclusion of intracranial hemorrhage and identification of large-vessel occlusion in both late and early time windows._

▪ _The extent of ischemic injury can be assessed by perfusion imaging, which allows identification of the ischemic core and salvageable penumbra._

▪ _Neuroimaging protocols for patient selection for thrombectomy must be optimized to meet institutional workflows and available equipment._

Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) has a current global incidence of 7.59 million cases [[1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R1)]. The emergence of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT), performed using either a stentriever or an aspiration catheter, revolutionized the care of patients with AIS with large-vessel occlusion (AIS-LVO) of the anterior circulation (i.e., of the internal carotid artery [ICA], the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery [MCA], or the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery [ACA]), and EVT is currently the standard-of-care treatment for appropriate candidates [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. Landmark trials that showed the efficacy of EVT represented a distinct departure from the historic treatment of patients with AIS [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. These studies incorporated the use of neuroimaging, most notably to confirm a large-vessel occlusion (LVO), to determine patient eligibility for EVT in both early (0–6 hours from symptom onset) and late (> 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset) time windows [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)].

Patients with AIS-LVO who are most likely to benefit from EVT have three characteristics on baseline neuroimaging: an LVO that is amenable to EVT; a small ischemic core (defined as the brain tissue considered to be likely infarcted); and critically hypoperfused brain tissue that, on the basis of the presence of an imaging or clinical mismatch, appears salvageable if recanalization of the occluded cervical or cerebral artery is achieved ([Fig. 1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F1A)). Patients with a cerebral hemorrhage at baseline typically are also excluded from treatment [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. Assessment for EVT in patients with AIS-LVO may use a variety of CT and MRI techniques and protocols; these should be optimized for each hospital's workflow to expedite patient treatment.

In this review, we describe common imaging modalities and recommended algorithms for the selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT. We also discuss emerging areas of expanded treatment by EVT that are likely to alter clinical practice in the next several years.

## Noninvasive Imaging Techniques

### _Detection of Large-Vessel Occlusion_

Accurate identification of an LVO is crucial to determine EVT eligibility. Prior studies that failed to find a benefit of EVT did not include CTA or MRA as part of the enrollment criteria, and a large percentage of patients who were evaluated lacked evidence of an LVO by digital subtraction angiography performed before EVT was attempted [[11](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R11)–[13](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R13)]. More recent successful EVT trials included identification of an LVO by CTA or MRA as part of the enrollment criteria [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)].

The most commonly performed study to identify the presence of an LVO is CTA [[14](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R14)–[16](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R16)]. Most centers perform CTA by acquiring a single-phase acquisition, which is sufficient to evaluate cerebral arterial vasculature. Multiphase CTA, which was used as part of patient selection in the ESCAPE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01778335) trial, is less commonly performed and acquires images in the peak arterial, venous, and late venous phases [[17](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R17)]. Multiphase CTA has shown potential in helping to differentiate proximal ICA occlusion from pseudoocclusion (i.e., a column of stagnate nonopacified blood proximal to a true intracranial occlusion or severe stenosis that results in the appearance of an ICA occlusion) [[18](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R18)].

In patients who undergo MRI rather than CT before EVT, MRA is used to identify the presence of an LVO. Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA is the most common technique. On the TOF sequence, static tissue signal is nulled by repeated radiofrequency pulses, whereas inflowing blood remains unsaturated and hyper-intense due to continued movement [[19](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R19)]. Although TOF MRA provides diagnostic information similar to that of CTA for the detection of LVOs, the method is limited by lack of coverage of neck and medium-to-distal intracranial vessels. Alternatively, contrast-enhanced MRA includes the neck vessels but would result in two separate doses of gadolinium-based contrast material in patients who later undergo perfusion MRI. There is a lack of strong evidence that vascular imaging of the neck influences thrombectomy treatment decisions, procedural times, or procedural success.

CT perfusion imaging (CTP) or perfusion MRI has shown the potential to identify the presence of an LVO in patients who do not undergo CTA or MRA. In a study of patients with AIS, the combination of perfusion MRI and DWI alone resulted in 95.9% sensitivity and 98.4% specificity for the correct triage of EVT as well as for highly accurate localization to the ICA M1 (96%) or M2 (90%) segment [[20](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R20)]. CTP has also shown potential in helping to identify occlusions in more distal small and medium vessels [[21](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R21), [22](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R22)]. These results require prospective validation, and CTA or MRA remain the standard of care for LVO detection. Nonetheless, neurointerventionalists and neurologists routinely apply CTP or perfusion MRI using mobile software platforms to identify patients with an LVO who may benefit from EVT treatment.

### _Ischemic Core Delineation_

_Qualitative assessment of ischemia on noncontrast CT—_ Noncontrast CT remains the most common first-line imaging modality for AIS evaluation due to its widespread availability and the speed of imaging. However, detection of ischemia with noncontrast CT remains challenging, with a reported sensitivity of 26–48% [[23](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R23), [24](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R24)]. Early signs of ischemia on noncontrast CT include loss of differentiation between gray matter and white matter, sulcal effacement, and hypoattenuation of the basal ganglia, caudate head, and insula [[25](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R25)–[27](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R27)]. When correctly detected, these signs of ischemia can be qualitatively applied to measure the degree of ischemic injury. However, noncontrast CT is not useful for accurate volumetric segmentation of the ischemic core, as is made possible by CTP or other advanced CT techniques or by diffusion-weighted MRI techniques. Brain tissue that shows hypoattenuation on noncontrast CT is highly likely to be irreversibly infarcted, and recovery of hypoattenuating brain tissue in patients with AIS-LVO is rare [[28](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R28)].

_Semiquantitative ischemic core assessment using the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score—_ The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) was developed as a method to standardize the assessment of ischemic injury on noncontrast CT [[29](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R29)]. ASPECTS divides the MCA territory into 10 separate regions and allocates 1 point per region. Points are removed when hypoattenuation is present within 50% or more of a region on noncontrast CT ([Fig. 2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F2A)). Currently, patients with LVO and an ASPECTS of 6 or greater are considered favorable candidates for EVT [[29](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R29)]. ASPECTS has proven to be effective for patient selection, as described later in this review, but the technique has poor interreader agreement [[29](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R29), [30](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R30)].

Although ASPECTS was a component of the imaging inclusion criteria in trials of thrombectomy at early time windows, it has not been used as part of imaging inclusion criteria in patients with AIS-LVO who present in the late time window (> 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset) [[5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R5), [6](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R6)]. The DEFUSE 3 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02586415) trial excluded from treatment those patients who had an ASPECTS of less than 6. Therefore, selection of patients for EVT when they present more than 6 hours after symptom onset still relies on CTP or MRI to determine the volume of the ischemic core. A post hoc analysis of the DEFUSE 3 trial, which included patients who were screened but not enrolled in the study, found that patients in the late time window who had an ASPECTS of 8–10 had small ischemic core volumes, whereas patients with an ASPECTS of 5–7 had highly variable ischemic core volumes [[31](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R31)]. These findings suggest that some patients with lower ASPECTS may not be favorable EVT candidates.

_Quantitative volumetric ischemic core assessment using CT perfusion imaging and DWI—_ DWI is an accurate and widely accepted technique for establishing ischemic core volume. DWI sequences are highly sensitive to the diffusion of water molecules in tissues. With the development of tissue ischemia, dysfunction of the sodium-potassium cell membrane pump due to loss of cellular energy results in restriction of water molecules and cellular swelling [[32](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R32)]. These changes correspond to hyperintense tissue on DWI and hypointense tissue on the ADC map [[33](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R33), [34](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R34)]. An ADC of less than 620 × 10−6 mm 2/s is considered the optimal threshold for delineation of the ischemic core [[35](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R35)]. Although increased signal on DWI at the recommended ADC threshold is clinically characterized as irreversibly infarcted tissue, this signal can be partially reversed, especially in early time windows; thus, the concept of the ischemic core is controversial [[36](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R36)].

Although DWI is a highly accurate method for delineating the ischemic core, MRI is less widely available, especially in the emergency department setting. Therefore, CT techniques that are capable of ischemic core identification and delineation have been developed over the years. CTP is the most commonly used technique for estimation of the ischemic core in patients with AISLVO. The ischemic core is commonly measured as a reduction in cerebral blood flow (CBF) of more than 70% or a significant reduction of cerebral blood volume (CBV) in the hemisphere affected by the stroke compared with the contralateral hemisphere [[37](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R37)]. Reduced CBF and CBV thresholds that best estimate the ischemic core vary by software platform, and commercial software is often purposely designed to underestimate the ischemic core volume to reduce the risk of inadvertent exclusion from EVT treatment [[37](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R37)]. Patients with AIS-LVO and an ischemic core volume of 50–70 mL or less are considered favorable candidates for EVT treatment [[7](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R7)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. Whether patients with larger ischemic core volumes also benefit from thrombectomy remains uncertain, and ongoing trials are testing whether these patients benefit from EVT.

Although CTP estimation of the ischemic core is accurate in most patients, CTP interpretation has numerous potential pitfalls [[38](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R38)]. The potential for overestimation of the ischemic core in patients presenting within the first 60–90 minutes after they were last known to be well and for underestimation of the ischemic core due to delayed collateral recruitment warrant particular attention, with noncontrast CT findings considered [[38](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R38)]. Given the potential variability of CTP results, the interpretation should be integrated with consideration of the patient's clinical status.

### _Penumbra Evaluation_

The penumbra represents the hypoperfused brain tissue that surrounds the ischemic core. The penumbra is salvageable if the occluded artery that is causing the stroke is recanalized to restore blood flow to the brain [[39](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R39)]. Therefore, salvage of the penumbra and assessment for a volume mismatch between the ischemic core and penumbra are at the foundation of selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT.

Quantification of the penumbra is possible by CTP, perfusion MRI, or other advanced MRI techniques such as arterial spin labeling. These imaging techniques produce quantitative and visual assessments of the penumbra that can be applied quickly and easily to assess patient eligibility for EVT treatment. Commercialized automated systems quantify perfusion data and present the ischemic core and penumbral volumes, allowing treating physicians to quickly determine whether the penumbra is sufficiently larger than the ischemic core to justify treatment ([Fig. 3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F3)). Typically, the volume of the penumbra should be at least 15 mL greater than the volume of the ischemic core, and the ratio of the penumbra volume to the ischemic core volume should be at least 1.2–1.8 [[40](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R40)].

The use of perfusion imaging to identify and quantify the penumbra is not universally adopted, and critics of the technique argue that perfusion imaging is not necessary and may exclude from EVT those patients who may benefit from such intervention. By contrast, the FRAME (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03875820) study provides evidence that the identification of the penumbra and of patients with a mismatch between core and penumbra, even in early time windows, may help to identify patients who are likely to benefit from EVT [[41](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R41)]. This prospective study acquired perfusion imaging before EVT in patients with AIS-LVO who were 0–6 hours from symptom onset. However, perfusion imaging was not processed or evaluated by the treating physicians before EVT, such that treatment decisions were not determined by the presence of a mismatch profile. Once the perfusion imaging was processed, patients who had a perfusion match profile without evidence of a salvageable penumbra were found to have significantly lower rates of good outcomes compared with patients with evidence of a salvageable penumbra.

Multiple imaging techniques may be used to delineate the penumbra. These techniques are associated with variable parameter maps and thresholds, depending on the vendor of the software that is used to process the perfusion data. This topic is discussed at greater depth by Vagal et al. [[38](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R38)].

Although CTP and perfusion MRI are important techniques to aid in patient selection for EVT in the setting of AIS-LVO, alternative techniques such as arterial spin labeling could help illustrate the presence and relative size of penumbra. In addition, mismatch between the core and clinical symptoms, whereby the volume of core infarct underrepresents the patient's clinical symptoms, was part of the inclusion criteria for the DAWN (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02142283) trial, and can be used to determine EVT eligibility [[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)].

## Imaging Algorithms for Thrombectomy Candidate Identification

The MR CLEAN (Netherlands Trial Registry number NTR1804) trial and the THRACE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01062698) trial were the first randomized trials to show the efficacy of EVT for patients with AIS-LVO, with both trials requiring noncontrast CT to rule out intracranial hemorrhage and with CTA or MRA required to identify an LVO [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3), [4](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R4)]. The REVASCAT (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01692379) trial used a more refined imaging algorithm for patient selection that included ASPECTS (ASPECTS of > 6 on noncontrast CT or > 5 on DWI) as well as CTA or MRA [[5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R5)]. REVASCAT found that EVT plus medical therapy led to higher rates of favorable outcomes compared with medical therapy alone in patients who presented within 8 hours from symptom onset, with a stronger treatment effect compared with the MR CLEAN trial [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3), [5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R5)].

The ESCAPE trial extended the treatment window for EVT to up to 12 hours from symptom onset by including patients with ASPECTS of 6 or greater and favorable arterial collaterals on CTA [[6](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R6)]. Patients were defined as having good-to-moderate collaterals on single-phase or multiphase CTA when filling of 50% or more of the MCA pial arterial circulation was shown, as compared with the normal contralateral side ([Fig. 4](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F4A)).

The EXTEND-IA (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01492725) and SWIFT PRIME (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01657461) studies incorporated the use of perfusion imaging for selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT up to 6 hours from symptom onset [[7](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R7), [8](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R8)]. The DEFUSE 3 and DAWN trials showed that EVT was superior to medical therapy alone for the treatment of AIS-LVO in eligible patients who were last known to be well from 6 to either 16 or 24 hours after symptom onset [[9](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R9), [10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. Both studies used perfusion imaging or DWI to quantify the ischemic core volumetrically. The DEFUSE 3 trial used the presence of mismatch by CTP or perfusion MRI to select patients for thrombectomy treatment. The DAWN trial inclusion criteria incorporated the presence of mismatch between the perfusion core and clinical symptoms. Details of the imaging criteria for these landmark trials are summarized in [Table 1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#tab1).

## Recommended Imaging Algorithms

Many reasonable imaging protocols can accurately and expeditiously identify potential EVT candidates, and each center should implement a workflow that is optimized for the individual hospital environment [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2), [42](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R42)]. For example, a hospital that acts as a central referral hub may require a different imaging algorithm and work-flow than the referring hospitals that it serves. This section presents a nonexhaustive set of suggested imaging algorithms.

### _Early Time Window (0–6 Hours From Symptom Onset)_

Several imaging algorithms are accepted for patients with AIS-LVO who present in early time windows [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. This imaging must exclude intracranial hemorrhage, identify the presence of an LVO, and provide at least a qualitative assessment of the degree of ischemic injury before consideration of EVT. At a minimum, patients should undergo noncontrast CT and CTA to determine EVT eligibility. A more complex imaging protocol that includes the application of ASPECTS, multiphase CTA for improved arterial collateral assessment, or CTP for ischemic core and target mismatch quantification is reasonable and is often used at U.S. stroke centers. MRI-based techniques such as MRA, DWI, and perfusion MRI may be used in place of CT at centers with rapid MRI access.

### _Late Time Window (> 6 to 24 Hours From Symptom Onset)_

The evaluation of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT in late time windows requires advanced imaging based on current guidelines [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. In late time windows, brain imaging must exclude the presence of intracranial hemorrhage, identify the presence of an LVO, quantify the ischemic core volume, and identify a mismatch between the ischemic core volume and either the penumbra volume or the severity of the patient's clinical deficits. At a minimum, patients should undergo noncontrast CT, CTA, and CTP or comparable MRI-based techniques, so their eligibility for EVT can be determined. It is reasonable to apply the DEFUSE 3 ischemic core criteria (i.e., ischemic core volume < 70 mL) to patients who present within 16 hours of symptom onset [[43](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R43)]. This same threshold is likely reasonable to apply in patients who present within 24 hours of symptom onset. However, the ischemic core volume at this later time of presentation varies by age, and the DAWN criteria are likely more accurate ([Table 1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#tab1)).

## Future Areas for Treatment Expansion

The success of stroke investigators in providing robust evidence that EVT is an effective therapy for AIS-LVO has revolutionized the treatment of eligible patients. However, much uncertainty remains as to whether other patients with AIS-LVO who fall outside the previously described clinical and imaging criteria may also benefit from EVT. Trials designed to expand treatment eligibility in patients with AIS-LVO are ongoing. In this section, we describe emerging areas of EVT treatment of ischemic stroke ([Fig. 5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F5)).
